## How to Brief and Sign Off a Website Designer in Pune: Nine Checkpoints From Wireframe to Launch

A good website designer in Pune is one you can hold to nine specific approval checkpoints: a written brief, a sitemap, wireframes, a design system, mobile-first page designs, real content, a build on staging, a pre-launch test pass and a post-launch review. Most disputes between a business and a designer do not come from bad taste on either side. They come from an approval that was never defined, so nobody can say afterwards whether the work was "done". This guide walks through each checkpoint, what you should have in your hands before you approve it, and what you should refuse to sign off on.

It is written for the person who will actually be on the client side of the project: a founder, a marketing manager, a trustee, a school administrator. You do not need to understand code. You need to know what to ask for and when.

### Why the process matters more than the portfolio

When people search for a website designer in Pune, they usually compare portfolios. A portfolio shows the best outcome of the best projects. It does not show how many revision rounds it took, how the designer handled a client who changed the brief in week three, or whether the site was still fast six months later. The process is the part you are actually buying, and it is the part you can inspect before you sign.

A useful test: ask the designer to describe the last project that went badly and what changed in their process afterwards. A studio with a real process has an answer. A studio without one will tell you nothing has ever gone wrong.

## Checkpoint 1: The written brief

Everything downstream depends on this document, and it should be short enough that both sides actually read it. One to two pages is plenty. It should answer:

- **Who is the visitor?** Not "everyone". Name two or three real visitor types, for example a parent comparing schools, a distributor checking your product range, a donor deciding whether to trust you with money.
- **What should each visitor do?** Call, fill a form, book a slot, donate, download a catalogue. One primary action per page.
- **What does success look like in three months?** Enquiries per month, share of enquiries from mobile, pages ranking for the phrases you care about. Pick measures you already track or can start tracking.
- **What exists today?** Current site address, analytics access, hosting, domain registrar, and any pages that already rank and must not lose their address.
- **What are the constraints?** Launch date tied to an event, brand guidelines, compliance text that legal must approve, integrations such as a CRM or a payment gateway.

If you do not yet have answers to some of these, say so in the brief and mark them open. A designer who accepts an incomplete brief silently will fill the gaps with guesses.

**Do not approve** a brief that says "modern, clean, professional". Those words describe nothing. Replace them with two or three reference sites you like and one sentence on what you like about each.

## Checkpoint 2: The sitemap and page inventory

Before any visual design, you should see a list of every page, how they connect, and what each is for. This is the cheapest stage at which to change your mind. Moving a box on a sitemap costs minutes; moving a page after it is designed and built costs days.

A page inventory for a typical service business might look like this:

| Page | Primary visitor | Primary action | Content owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Home | New visitor from search | Reach a service page | Marketing |
| Each service page | Buyer comparing options | Enquire / WhatsApp | Marketing |
| About | Buyer checking credibility | Read team and address, then enquire | Founder |
| Case studies | Buyer wanting proof | Enquire | Sales |
| Contact | Ready buyer | Call, form, map | Operations |
| Blog / guides | Researcher | Read, then move to a service page | Marketing |

Notice the last column. Every page needs a named person who will supply and approve its content. Sites are late far more often because content is late than because design is slow.

**Check that** the sitemap gives each service its own page rather than one long "Services" page. Separate pages can rank separately, and they let you send a specific link in an ad or a WhatsApp message. If you are unsure how to split services, our [website creation service](/services/website-creation) page shows how we structure service pages.

**Also check** that pages you already have ranking in Google keep an equivalent. If an old page is being removed or its address changes, the designer must list it for redirects. We cover the mechanics in [how to migrate a website without losing SEO](/blog/website-migration-without-seo-loss).

## Checkpoint 3: Wireframes

A wireframe is a grey-box sketch of a page: where the headline sits, where the form goes, how the sections stack. It has no colours, no photographs and no brand fonts, and that is deliberate. It stops you arguing about a shade of blue when the real question is whether the enquiry form is visible without scrolling.

Ask for wireframes of at least the home page, one service page and the contact page, in both a phone layout and a desktop layout. Then review them against the brief with three questions:

1. **Can a first-time visitor say what this business does within five seconds?** Cover the logo and read only the top of the page.
2. **Is the primary action visible on the first screen on a phone?** Most Indian business traffic arrives on mobile, so the phone layout is the real design and the desktop layout is the adaptation.
3. **Does every section earn its space?** Sliders that auto-rotate, giant hero videos and five-column footers with 40 links usually serve the designer's portfolio rather than your visitor.

**Do not approve** wireframes that contain lorem ipsum in the headings. Placeholder headings hide the hardest part of design, which is fitting your real words into the layout. A headline that is two lines in the sketch and five lines in reality will break the page.

## Checkpoint 4: The design system

Before the designer produces every page, they should show you the building blocks: the type scale, the colour palette with contrast checked, the button styles, the form styles, the spacing rules, the icon style. This is called a design system, and even a ten-page site benefits from one.

Why it matters to you:

- **Consistency without effort.** When you add a page later, it will look like the rest of the site, because the pieces already exist.
- **Accessibility built in.** Text and background colour pairs can be checked against the WCAG contrast guidance once, at this stage, instead of being patched after launch. If accessibility matters to your audience, see our [WCAG accessibility checklist for Indian sites](/blog/wcag-accessibility-checklist-india).
- **Faster future changes.** Adding a new service page becomes assembling existing blocks rather than commissioning fresh design.

**Ask** for the fonts to be named and licensed, and for a check that they support every script you need. A site for a Marathi or Hindi audience needs a Devanagari-capable font, and a font that looks lovely in Latin can fall back to an ugly default for Devanagari if nobody tested it. For multi-language builds, see [multilingual website considerations](/blog/multilingual-ngo-website-india-2026).

## Checkpoint 5: Page designs, mobile first

Now the designer applies the design system to your wireframes and produces high-fidelity mockups. Insist on seeing the phone version first, at a realistic width around 360 to 390 pixels, not only a laptop mockup shrunk down.

Review each page for these specifics:

**Tap targets and forms.** Buttons and links should be large enough to press with a thumb without hitting a neighbour. Forms should ask for the minimum: name, phone, one line about the need. Every extra field lowers completion, so justify each one.

**The thumb zone.** Sticky call or WhatsApp buttons at the bottom of a phone screen are common on Indian business sites because they match how people already contact businesses. Make sure they do not cover the content or the cookie notice.

**Real photographs.** Stock photography of smiling people at laptops adds nothing and can hurt trust. If you cannot afford a shoot for every page, prioritise a real team photo and real premises or product photos on the home, about and contact pages.

**Proof near the action.** Testimonials, accreditation logos or a physical address should sit close to the button they support. Only use testimonials and logos you have permission to display. Never let a designer invent or "fill in" a review to make a mockup look complete, because those placeholders have a way of shipping.

**Do not approve** a design whose text is set as part of an image. Text that is baked into a picture cannot be read by search engines or screen readers, cannot be translated and does not resize. Headlines should be live text.

## Checkpoint 6: Real content, in place

Content is the checkpoint most often skipped, and its absence is why launches slip. Before development starts, the actual headings and body text for the key pages should exist, not in a separate document that will be "pasted in later" but placed into the design.

A content checklist for each page:

- One `h1` heading that says what the page is about, containing the phrase a buyer would actually search.
- A short opening paragraph that answers the visitor's question directly.
- Descriptive `alt` text for meaningful images.
- A unique page title and meta description, written as a sentence for a person, not a list of keywords.
- Internal links to the next logical page.

Who writes it matters less than whether it is specific. A page that says "We provide best quality services at affordable price" could belong to anyone and ranks for nothing. A page that names the actual services, the neighbourhoods served, the process and the address does real work. For the search side of this, see our overview of [local SEO for Pune businesses](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026).

## Checkpoint 7: The build on staging

The designer's work now becomes a working site, but on a private staging address, not on your live domain. You should be able to click through every page on your own phone.

Give the staging site a proper review pass, not a glance:

1. **Every link and button.** Click each one. Confirm the phone number opens the dialler and the WhatsApp link opens the right number.
2. **Every form.** Submit a test enquiry and confirm it arrives at the right inbox, and that you receive whatever confirmation the visitor receives. Confirm spam protection does not block real submissions.
3. **Two phones and two browsers at minimum.** An older Android phone on a slow connection is a fairer test than the newest iPhone on office Wi-Fi.
4. **Text scaling.** Increase the phone's font size and confirm nothing overlaps.
5. **The 404 page.** Type a wrong address and check the visitor lands somewhere helpful.

Insist on a **noindex** setting on staging so the unfinished site does not appear in Google, and make sure it is removed at launch. The failure in the other direction, where a live site accidentally launches with a leftover "discourage search engines" setting, is common and costly. It is worth a dedicated line in your launch checklist. Our guide to [staging environments before launch](/blog/website-staging-before-launch) covers the setup.

## Checkpoint 8: The pre-launch test pass

This is the formal gate. A designer or developer should hand you a written record of checks, and you should hold the launch if items fail.

**Performance.** Google's published thresholds for a "good" experience are a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, assessed at the 75th percentile of real visitors (see [web.dev on Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)). Lab tests before launch only estimate real-user results, but a site that fails badly in the lab will fail in the field. Ask for the report and ask what was fixed. Our [website speed optimisation guide](/blog/website-speed-optimization-india-business) explains the usual causes.

**Search basics.** Confirm the XML sitemap exists and lists live pages, the robots file does not block important sections, page titles are unique, canonical tags point to the right address, and redirects from old addresses work.

**Analytics and conversion tracking.** Confirm the analytics tag fires, and that form submissions, phone clicks and WhatsApp clicks are recorded as conversions. If you launch without tracking, you lose the baseline you needed to judge the redesign. See [GA4 setup for Indian sites](/blog/ga4-conversion-tracking-setup-india).

**Legal and policy pages.** Privacy policy, terms and cookie information should be present and accurate for what the site really collects. Where your forms collect personal data, review our note on [DPDP Act website compliance](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026) with your legal adviser.

**Backups and security.** Confirm backups run and that you know how to restore one. Confirm admin accounts use strong unique passwords and, where available, two-factor authentication.

## Checkpoint 9: The post-launch review

Launch is not the end. Agree, in the contract, a review one to two weeks after launch and another at about three months.

At the first review, look for what only real traffic reveals: pages returning errors in Google Search Console, forms that did not deliver, unexpectedly slow pages on specific devices, and any drop in indexed pages. At the three-month review, go back to the success measures in your brief and compare.

Clarify before signing what the warranty covers. A fair arrangement is that defects against the agreed scope are fixed at no charge for a stated period, while new features are quoted separately. Clarify also who owns the source files, the design files and the accounts. Our guide on [contract ownership and warranty terms](/blog/web-development-company-pune-contract-ownership-warranty-2026) lists the clauses to look for.

## Handling revisions without wrecking the project

Revision rounds are where budgets and relationships quietly break down. Set the rules at the start:

- **Consolidated feedback.** One person on your side collects comments from everyone and sends a single list. Five people sending five emails guarantees contradictions.
- **A defined number of rounds per checkpoint.** Two is common. More than that usually signals that the brief was unclear, which is a problem to fix upstream, not with round three.
- **Change requests in writing.** A request that changes scope, such as a new page or a new integration, is a change request with its own estimate, not a "revision".
- **Approvals are approvals.** Once you sign off wireframes, moving the layout at the design stage is a change, not a correction. Designers who accept unlimited changes rarely deliver on time; designers who refuse all changes are unpleasant. The written rules protect both.

## Red flags to watch for when choosing a designer

- **No named person.** You cannot find out who will design and who will build.
- **Templates presented as custom design.** Templates are fine when honest and priced accordingly. The problem is paying custom rates for a reskinned theme.
- **No staging site.** Work is done directly on a live domain or shown only as screenshots.
- **Vague scope.** Phrases like "unlimited pages" or "all features included" with no page list.
- **Guaranteed rankings.** Nobody can promise a position on Google. Anyone who does is guessing or misleading you.
- **Ownership tied to continued payment.** You should own your domain, hosting account and content from day one.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long does it take to design and launch a business website?

It depends on scope and on how fast you supply content and feedback. A small brochure site with a handful of pages can move from brief to launch in a few weeks when content is ready; larger builds with custom features or integrations take longer. The most common cause of delay is late content and slow consolidated feedback, not design time.

### What should I give a website designer before the project starts?

Give them a one to two page brief, your current site address and analytics access, brand assets such as the logo and colours, reference sites you like, the pages you expect, and the person who will approve content. Also give them the list of integrations you need, such as a CRM, payment gateway or WhatsApp number.

### Should a website designer in Pune also handle SEO?

Basic on-page SEO belongs in the design and build: unique titles, headings, image alt text, clean URLs, a sitemap and fast pages. Ongoing SEO such as content planning, link building and reporting is a separate, continuing service and should be scoped and priced separately.

### Who owns the website after it is built?

You should. Confirm in writing that you own the domain, the hosting account, the final design files and the content, and that you receive all login details at handover. Ownership that depends on paying a monthly fee is a red flag.

### Do I need a mobile app as well as a mobile-friendly website?

For most service businesses, a fast, well-built mobile website is the first requirement, and an app is only justified if you need features a browser handles poorly. We discuss the trade-off in [mobile app or mobile-optimised website](/blog/web-development-company-pune-mobile-app-vs-website-2026).

## Where to Start

Write the one-page brief first, even if it takes an evening. Then list your pages, name a content owner for each and choose a reference site or two. With those three documents in hand, any conversation with a designer becomes specific.
